title: Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients
summary: Describes the authorization code interception attack against OAuth 2.0 public clients, such as mobile apps, and a technique to prevent it. The client creates a secret for each request and proves it knows that secret when redeeming the code, so a stolen code alone is useless.

plainLanguage.summary: PKCE, the Proof Key for Code Exchange, protects OAuth apps that cannot keep a secret, such as apps on a phone. The app makes a random secret for each sign-in, sends only a scrambled version of it with the request, and sends the real secret when it collects the result. An attacker who copies the code cannot redeem it, because the attacker never had the secret.

questions: how does pkce prevent authorization code interception
why do oauth public clients need pkce
s256 vs plain code challenge method
what is the difference between s256 and plain
subtitle: A one-time secret that stops a stolen OAuth authorization code from being redeemed by an attacker.

tldr.problem: An OAuth 2.0 public client, such as a mobile app, receives its authorization code through a redirect that an attacker on the same device can watch. The stolen code is enough to get an access token, because the client cannot keep a secret.
tldr.mechanism: The client creates a random code verifier for each request and sends only a transformed version, the code challenge, with the authorization request. When it redeems the code it also sends the verifier, and the server checks that transforming the verifier reproduces the challenge it recorded.
tldr.outcome: A stolen authorization code cannot be redeemed without the one-time verifier, which never leaves the client over an unprotected path. The document is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7636 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2015, and it has not been obsoleted. It adds two parameters to the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Request and one to the token request defined in RFC 6749, without changing any server response.

sections.title: The Authorization Code Interception Attack
sections.content:
OAuth 2.0 public clients are susceptible to the authorization code interception attack. In this attack the attacker intercepts the authorization code returned from the authorization endpoint within a communication path not protected by Transport Layer Security, such as inter-application communication inside the client's operating system. Once the attacker has the authorization code, it can use it to obtain the access token.

Figure 1 shows the attack. In step 1, the native application on the end device issues an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Request through the browser or operating system, and the Redirection Endpoint URI in this case typically uses a custom URI scheme. Step 1 happens through a secure API that cannot be intercepted, though it may potentially be observed in advanced attack scenarios. The request is forwarded to the OAuth 2.0 authorization server in step 2, and because OAuth requires the use of TLS, this communication is protected and cannot be intercepted. The authorization server returns the authorization code in step 3, and in step 4 the code is returned to the requester through the Redirection Endpoint URI provided in step 1.

It is possible for a malicious app to register itself as a handler for the custom scheme in addition to the legitimate app. Once it does so, the malicious app can intercept the authorization code in step 4, which lets the attacker request and obtain an access token in steps 5 and 6.

Several pre-conditions have to hold for the attack to work. The attacker must manage to register a malicious application on the client device and register a custom URI scheme that is also used by another application, and the operating system must allow a custom URI scheme to be registered by multiple applications. The OAuth 2.0 authorization code grant must be used. The attacker must have access to the client_id and client_secret, if provisioned; all native app client instances use the same client_id, and secrets provisioned in client binary applications cannot be considered confidential. Finally, one of two conditions holds. Either the attacker can observe only the responses from the authorization endpoint, in which case the plain code challenge method is enough to mitigate the attack, or the attacker can also observe the requests, for example because HTTP log information leaked in the operating system, in which case the code challenge method must be S256 or a value defined by a cryptographically secure extension.

The described attack has been observed in the wild and has to be considered in OAuth 2.0 deployments. The OAuth 2.0 threat model describes mitigation techniques, but they are not applicable here because they rely on a per-client instance secret or a per-client instance redirect URI.
sections.plainLanguage: On a phone, a sign-in usually returns to the app through a link that the operating system hands to whichever app claims it. A second app can claim the same link, receive the authorization code, and exchange it for an access token. The problem is that an app on a device cannot keep a secret, so the code alone has to be enough for the attacker.

sections.title: Abstract Protocol Flow
sections.content:
This specification adds parameters to the OAuth 2.0 Authorization and Access Token Requests, shown in abstract form in Figure 2.

In step A, the client creates and records a secret named the code verifier, and derives a transformed version, written as t(code_verifier) and referred to as the code challenge, which is sent in the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Request along with the transformation method, written as t_m.

In step B, the authorization endpoint responds as usual but records t(code_verifier) and the transformation method.

In step C, the client sends the authorization code in the Access Token Request as usual, but includes the code verifier secret generated at step A.

In step D, the authorization server transforms the code verifier and compares it to the t(code_verifier) from step B. Access is denied if they are not equal.

An attacker who intercepts the authorization code at step B is unable to redeem it for an access token, because the attacker does not have the code verifier secret.
sections.plainLanguage: The flow has four steps. The client sends a scrambled form of its secret with the authorization request. The server stores that scrambled form with the code it issues. The client sends the code and the real secret to the token endpoint. The server scrambles the secret again and compares the two, and only hands out a token if they match.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
In addition to the terms defined in OAuth 2.0, this specification defines four terms. A code verifier is a cryptographically random string used to correlate the authorization request to the token request. A code challenge is a challenge derived from the code verifier that is sent in the authorization request, to be verified against later. A code challenge method is a method that was used to derive the code challenge. Base64url encoding is base64 encoding using the URL- and filename-safe character set defined in Section 5 of RFC 4648, with all trailing equals signs omitted and without the inclusion of any line breaks, whitespace or other additional characters.

The document uses the Augmented Backus-Naur Form notation of RFC 5234. STRING denotes a sequence of zero or more ASCII characters, OCTETS a sequence of zero or more octets, ASCII(STRING) the octets of the ASCII representation of that string, BASE64URL-ENCODE(OCTETS) the base64url encoding of those octets, BASE64URL-DECODE(STRING) the reverse, and SHA256(OCTETS) a SHA2 256-bit hash of those octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Two names matter. The code verifier is the secret the client keeps. The code challenge is the value derived from it that travels in the request. A code challenge method says how the derivation is done.

sections.title: Creating the Code Verifier and the Code Challenge
sections.content:
The client first creates a code verifier for each OAuth 2.0 Authorization Request. It is a high-entropy cryptographic random string using the unreserved characters A-Z, a-z, 0-9, hyphen, period, underscore and tilde from Section 2.3 of RFC 3986, with a minimum length of 43 characters and a maximum length of 128 characters. The ABNF is code-verifier = 43*128unreserved.

The code verifier should have enough entropy to make it impractical to guess the value. It is recommended that the output of a suitable random number generator be used to create a 32-octet sequence, which is then base64url-encoded to produce a 43-octet URL safe string to use as the code verifier.

The client then creates a code challenge from the verifier with one of two transformations. With plain, the code challenge is the code verifier itself. With S256, the code challenge is BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier))). If the client is capable of using S256, it must use S256, because S256 is Mandatory To Implement on the server. Clients are permitted to use plain only if they cannot support S256 for some technical reason and know through out-of-band configuration that the server supports plain. The plain transformation is for compatibility with existing deployments and for constrained environments that cannot use the S256 transformation. The ABNF for the code challenge is the same shape as for the verifier, code-challenge = 43*128unreserved.

The client sends the code challenge as part of the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Request using two additional parameters. The code_challenge parameter is required. The code_challenge_method parameter is optional and defaults to plain if it is not present in the request, and its value is S256 or plain.
sections.plainLanguage: The verifier is a random string of 43 to 128 characters drawn from letters, digits and a few safe symbols. The recommended way to make it is to generate 32 random bytes and encode them, which gives a 43-character string. The challenge is then either that string unchanged, or its SHA-256 hash written in base64url. A client that can compute the hash must use it.

sections.title: Issuing the Code and Checking the Verifier
sections.content:
When the server issues the authorization code in the authorization response, it must associate the code_challenge and code_challenge_method values with the code so they can be verified later. Typically those values are stored in encrypted form in the code itself, but they could alternatively be stored on the server associated with the code. The server must not include the code_challenge value in client requests in a form that other entities can extract, and the exact method used to associate the challenge with the code is out of scope for the specification.

If the server requires PKCE and the client does not send the code_challenge in the request, the authorization endpoint must return the authorization error response with the error value set to invalid_request, and the error_description or error_uri should explain the nature of the error, for example that a code challenge is required. If the server supports PKCE but does not support the requested transformation, the authorization endpoint must return the same invalid_request error, with a description such as transform algorithm not supported.

Upon receipt of the authorization code, the client sends the Access Token Request to the token endpoint, adding one parameter to those defined in OAuth 2.0: the code_verifier, which is required. The code_challenge_method is bound to the authorization code when the code is issued, and that is the method the token endpoint must use to verify the code_verifier.

On receipt of the request at the token endpoint, the server verifies it by calculating the code challenge from the received code_verifier and comparing it with the previously associated code_challenge, after first transforming it according to the code_challenge_method specified by the client. If the method was S256, the received verifier is hashed by SHA-256, base64url-encoded, and compared to the code_challenge, that is BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier))) equals code_challenge. If the method was plain, they are compared directly, that is code_verifier equals code_challenge. If the values are equal, the token endpoint must continue processing as normal. If they are not equal, an error response indicating invalid_grant must be returned.
sections.plainLanguage: The server remembers the challenge with the code it issues, either inside the code itself or on the server. When the client comes back with the code, it also sends the verifier, and the server derives the challenge again and compares. A mismatch means the caller did not make the original request, and the answer is an error rather than a token.

sections.title: Compatibility
sections.content:
Server implementations of this specification may accept OAuth 2.0 clients that do not implement the extension. If the code_verifier is not received from the client in the Authorization Request, servers supporting backwards compatibility revert to the OAuth 2.0 protocol without this extension.

Because the OAuth 2.0 server responses are unchanged by this specification, client implementations do not need to know whether the server has implemented it, and should send the additional parameters defined in Section 4 to all servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing in the server's replies changes, so a client can send the extra parameters to every server without checking first. A server that does not support the extension ignores them, and a server that does support it but receives no verifier falls back to the older behaviour.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Entropy of the code verifier. The security model relies on the code verifier not being learned or guessed by the attacker, so it has to be created in a manner that is cryptographically random and has high entropy that makes guessing impractical. The client should create a code_verifier with a minimum of 256 bits of entropy, which can be done by having a suitable random number generator create a 32-octet sequence that is then base64url-encoded to produce a 43-octet URL safe string.

Protection against eavesdroppers. Clients must not downgrade to plain after trying the S256 method. Servers that support PKCE are required to support S256, and servers that do not support PKCE simply ignore the unknown code_verifier, so an error when S256 is presented can only mean that the server is faulty or that a man-in-the-middle attacker is trying a downgrade attack. The S256 method protects against eavesdroppers observing or intercepting the code_challenge, because the challenge cannot be used without the verifier. With the plain method there is a chance that the code_challenge is observed by the attacker on the device or in the HTTP request; because the code challenge is then the same as the code verifier, plain does not protect against eavesdropping of the initial request. Plain should not be used and exists only for compatibility with deployed implementations where the request path is already protected, and should not be used in new implementations unless they cannot support S256 for some technical reason. If the code challenge method is plain and the challenge is to be returned inside the authorization code to achieve a stateless server, it must be encrypted so that only the server can decrypt and extract it.

Salting the code_challenge. To reduce implementation complexity, salting is not used, because the code verifier contains sufficient entropy to prevent brute-force attacks. Concatenating a publicly known value to a code verifier and then hashing it with SHA-256 would not increase the number of attempts necessary to brute force a valid verifier. The S256 transformation resembles hashing a password, but there are important differences: passwords tend to be relatively low-entropy words that can be hashed offline and the hash looked up in a dictionary, and salting them greatly expands the dictionary space an attacker must search. Modern graphics processors let attackers calculate hashes in real time faster than they could be looked up from a disk, which removes the value of the salt in increasing the complexity of a brute-force attack even for low-entropy passwords.

All the OAuth security analysis presented in RFC 6819 applies, so readers should follow it carefully. Current security considerations for TLS and DTLS are found in BCP 195, RFC 7525, which supersedes the TLS version recommendations in OAuth 2.0.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole scheme rests on the verifier being unguessable, so it needs at least 256 bits of real randomness. The hashed method is what protects the verifier itself, and a client must not fall back to the unprotected method after the hashed one fails, because that failure is what a downgrade attack looks like. No salt is needed, because a verifier is not a low-entropy password.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Three parameters are registered in the IANA OAuth Parameters registry defined in OAuth 2.0. The code_verifier parameter is used in the token request, the code_challenge parameter in the authorization request, and the code_challenge_method parameter in the authorization request. The change controller for all three is the IESG and the specification document is this RFC.

The document also establishes a PKCE Code Challenge Methods registry, a sub-registry of the OAuth Parameters registry. Additional code_challenge_method types are registered using the Specification Required policy of RFC 5226, which includes review of the request by one or more Designated Experts. The Designated Experts ensure that there is at least a two-week review of the request on the oauth-ext-review mailing list and that any discussion converges before they respond. To allow values to be allocated before publication, the Designated Experts may approve a registration once satisfied that an acceptable specification will be published. They should consider the discussion on the mailing list and the overall security properties of the challenge method, and new methods should not disclose the value of the code verifier in the request to the authorization endpoint. A denial should include an explanation and, where applicable, suggestions for how to make the request successful.

The registration template asks for the parameter name, which is case-sensitive, should be short, not exceeding 8 characters without a compelling reason, and may not match another registered name in a case-insensitive manner unless the Designated Experts allow an exception. It also asks for the change controller, which is IESG for Standards Track RFCs, and for the specification document.

The initial registry contents are the two method parameter names defined in Section 4.2, plain and S256, both with the IESG as change controller and with Section 4.2 of this document as the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Three OAuth parameter names and two challenge method names are registered, so that every implementation uses the same words. New challenge methods go through a review by designated experts, and a new method must not reveal the verifier.
